stem: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in which year, after which he became the central figure of the nationalist movement?
solution: Mahatma Gandhi returned to India in 1915 from South Africa, where he had lived for over two decades and developed his techniques of mass mobilisation and satyagraha (non-violent resistance) while fighting racial discrimination against Indians there. On returning, he gradually became the central figure of the Indian national movement. So he returned in 1915. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: In South Africa, Gandhi had developed and practised his distinctive method of non-violent protest, which he called __________.
solution: In South Africa, Gandhi developed and practised the method he called SATYAGRAHA — literally 'insistence on/devotion to truth' (satya = truth, agraha = insistence). It was a technique of NON-VIOLENT resistance and mass struggle based on truth, moral force, and the willingness to suffer for a just cause (without hatred or violence toward the opponent). He first forged this method in the struggles against racial discrimination in South Africa and later applied it in India. So his method was satyagraha. This is a foundational concept.

stem: On the advice of his political mentor, __________, Gandhi spent his first year back in India travelling around the country to understand its people and conditions before taking up active politics.
solution: On the advice of his political mentor Gopal Krishna Gokhale (a senior moderate leader of the Congress), Gandhi spent his first year back in India (1915–16) TRAVELLING widely across the country to see and understand its people, their conditions, and their problems — before plunging into active politics. Gokhale advised him to first acquaint himself with India. So his mentor was Gopal Krishna Gokhale. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Gandhi's first major satyagraha in India (1917) was on behalf of the indigo cultivators of __________ in Bihar.
solution: Gandhi's first major satyagraha in India was the Champaran satyagraha of 1917, in the Champaran district of Bihar. There he took up the cause of the INDIGO cultivators (peasants), who were being oppressed by European planters under the 'tinkathia' system (compelled to grow indigo on part of their land on unfair terms). Gandhi's intervention led to an enquiry and relief for the peasants. So his first Indian satyagraha was at Champaran (1917). This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: In 1918, Gandhi undertook satyagraha in __________ (Gujarat) in support of peasants seeking remission of land revenue after crop failure, and also intervened in a mill-workers' dispute at Ahmedabad.
solution: In 1918, Gandhi led a satyagraha in the Kheda district of Gujarat in support of the PEASANTS, who, facing crop failure, were demanding remission (suspension) of the land revenue that the government was insisting on collecting. In the same year he also intervened in the Ahmedabad mill-workers' dispute (undertaking a fast on their behalf). These early struggles (Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda) established Gandhi's methods and reputation in India. So the 1918 peasant satyagraha was at Kheda. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The repressive law of 1919 that allowed detention of political suspects without trial, and which Gandhi launched a satyagraha against, was the __________.
solution: The Rowlatt Act (1919) was a repressive law that empowered the government to imprison/detain political suspects WITHOUT TRIAL. It provoked widespread anger, and Gandhi launched a nationwide satyagraha (the Rowlatt Satyagraha) against it in 1919 — his first attempt at an all-India mass agitation, involving strikes (hartals) and protests. So the 1919 repressive law was the Rowlatt Act. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The horrific massacre of unarmed civilians at __________ in Amritsar, on 13 April 1919, deeply shocked the nation during the anti-Rowlatt agitation.
solution: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre occurred on 13 April 1919 at Amritsar (Punjab), when General Dyer ordered troops to fire on a large, unarmed crowd gathered in an enclosed garden (Jallianwala Bagh), killing and wounding hundreds. This atrocity, during the anti-Rowlatt agitation, deeply shocked and angered the nation and became a turning point, intensifying anti-British feeling. So the massacre was at Jallianwala Bagh. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: The first great mass movement led by Gandhi (1920–22), which combined the Khilafat cause with the demand for swaraj and involved boycotting British institutions, was the __________.
solution: The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) was the first great mass movement led by Gandhi. It called on Indians to NON-COOPERATE with the British government — boycotting British goods, schools, colleges, law courts, titles, and councils — and it was combined with the KHILAFAT cause (support for the Ottoman Caliph, uniting Hindus and Muslims). Its aim was to attain SWARAJ (self-rule). It marked the transformation of the national movement into a mass struggle. So the 1920–22 movement was the Non-Cooperation Movement. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Gandhi abruptly called off the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922 following the violent incident at __________, where a mob killed policemen.
solution: Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922 after the violent incident at Chauri Chaura (in the United Provinces/present-day UP), where an angry mob of protesters clashed with police and set fire to a police station, killing about 22 policemen. Because the movement had turned violent — contrary to his principle of NON-VIOLENCE — Gandhi decided to suspend/withdraw the movement. So the incident that led him to call off Non-Cooperation was at Chauri Chaura. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The Civil Disobedience Movement began in 1930 with Gandhi's famous march to __________ to break the salt law.
solution: The Civil Disobedience Movement began in 1930 with Gandhi's famous Salt March (Dandi March): he marched about 240 miles (over some 24 days) from his Sabarmati Ashram to the coastal village of DANDI (in Gujarat), where, on 6 April 1930, he broke the SALT LAW by making salt from seawater — defying the British government's monopoly/tax on salt. This act of symbolic defiance launched the nationwide Civil Disobedience Movement. So the march was to Dandi. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: Gandhi chose SALT as the focus of the 1930 movement because __________.
options: Salt was consumed by everyone (rich and poor alike), and the tax/monopoly on this basic necessity symbolised the injustice and oppressiveness of British rule — making it a powerful unifying issue
Salt was very expensive to produce
The British had no interest in salt
solution: Gandhi chose SALT as the focus because it was a brilliant, unifying issue: salt is a BASIC NECESSITY consumed by EVERYONE — rich and poor, of all regions and religions — yet the British held a MONOPOLY on its production and levied a TAX on it, even though people could easily make salt from the sea. This tax on an essential item that no one could do without symbolised the INJUSTICE and oppressiveness of British rule in a way ordinary people could immediately grasp and feel. Breaking the salt law was therefore a simple, powerful, and universally relatable act of defiance that could mobilise the masses. So salt was chosen because it affected everyone and symbolised British injustice. So option 1 is correct.

stem: One of the most important CONSEQUENCES of Gandhi's leadership was that he transformed the national movement into __________.
options: A mass movement — drawing in peasants, workers, women, and ordinary people (not just the educated elite)
A movement of only lawyers and landlords
A movement confined to the cities
solution: A crucial consequence of Gandhi's leadership was the TRANSFORMATION of the national movement from a largely ELITE affair (dominated by educated professionals and the well-to-do) into a genuine MASS MOVEMENT. Through his methods, simple message, and symbols (like khadi and salt), and his identification with the poor, Gandhi drew vast numbers of ordinary Indians into the struggle — PEASANTS, WORKERS, WOMEN, students, and people of all classes and regions. This mass participation gave the freedom movement its enormous strength and legitimacy. So Gandhi transformed it into a mass movement. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Gandhi laid great emphasis on the spinning wheel (charkha) and the wearing of __________ as symbols of self-reliance and dignity of labour.
solution: Gandhi laid great emphasis on the spinning wheel (charkha) and on the wearing of KHADI — hand-spun and hand-woven cloth. To him, spinning and khadi symbolised SELF-RELIANCE (economic independence from British machine-made textiles), the DIGNITY of manual LABOUR, the unity of the nation, and a bridge between rich and poor and between mental and physical work. The charkha became a powerful symbol of the movement (and appeared on the Congress flag). So the cloth was khadi. This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: Gandhi worked for the upliftment of the so-called 'untouchables', whom he called __________, campaigning against untouchability.
solution: Gandhi worked for the upliftment of the so-called 'untouchables' (the depressed castes), whom he called 'HARIJANS', meaning 'children of God'. He campaigned vigorously AGAINST untouchability, regarding its removal as essential to the moral regeneration of India and to national unity, and he undertook fasts and constructive work toward this end. So he called them Harijans. (Note: B.R. Ambedkar and many in the community preferred the term 'Dalit' and had important differences with Gandhi over approach and political representation.) This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: The Quit India Movement, the last great mass movement led by Gandhi, was launched in which year with the slogan 'Do or Die'?
solution: The Quit India Movement was launched in August 1942, when Gandhi and the Congress demanded an END to British rule ('Quit India'). Gandhi gave the famous call/slogan 'Do or Die' (karo ya maro) — urging Indians to struggle for freedom, either to free India or to die in the attempt (while remaining non-violent). It was the last great mass movement of the freedom struggle and, though quickly suppressed with mass arrests, it demonstrated the depth of the demand for independence. So Quit India was launched in 1942. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: The chapter emphasises the importance of studying newspapers, letters, and autobiographies to understand Gandhi. A special value of PRIVATE letters and autobiographies is that they __________.
options: Reveal the personal thoughts, feelings, and inner life of the writer (though they too are shaped by the writer's perspective and self-presentation, and must be read critically)
Are always perfectly objective and complete
solution: The chapter (which is partly about how we KNOW about Gandhi and the movement) emphasises varied sources — newspapers, government records, letters, and autobiographies. A special value of PRIVATE letters and AUTOBIOGRAPHIES is that they can reveal the PERSONAL THOUGHTS, FEELINGS, motivations, and inner life of the writer — offering an intimate, first-person perspective not found in official records. However, historians caution that these too are SHAPED by the writer's own viewpoint and by conscious SELF-PRESENTATION (a person writing about themselves may idealise, justify, or select), so they must be read CRITICALLY, not as transparent truth. So autobiographies/letters reveal personal thoughts but must be read critically. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Newspapers of the time are valuable sources for studying Gandhi and the movement, but they must be used carefully because __________.
options: Different newspapers (nationalist, British-owned, regional) reported events from their own viewpoints, so they present partial and sometimes biased accounts that must be cross-checked
All newspapers reported identically and neutrally
Newspapers were written only in English
solution: Newspapers (published in English and various Indian languages) are valuable sources for studying Gandhi and the national movement — reporting his activities, speeches, and the events of the movement, and reflecting public opinion. But they must be used CAREFULLY, because DIFFERENT newspapers reported from their own VIEWPOINTS: nationalist/Indian-owned papers tended to be sympathetic to Gandhi and the movement, while British-owned or pro-government papers were often hostile or dismissive; and each selected and framed events according to its stance. So newspaper accounts are PARTIAL and sometimes BIASED, and historians must read them critically and CROSS-CHECK them against other sources. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Gandhi's ability to communicate with and mobilise the masses was greatly helped by __________.
options: His simple lifestyle, dress, and language, and his use of everyday symbols (like khadi and salt) and religious/moral idioms that ordinary people understood
His use of complex English legal arguments only
His refusal to meet ordinary people
His reliance solely on foreign supporters
solution: Gandhi's remarkable ability to connect with and mobilise the MASSES owed much to his SIMPLE lifestyle, DRESS (the loincloth/dhoti and khadi, like the poorest peasant), and LANGUAGE, and to his use of everyday SYMBOLS (the charkha, khadi, salt) and religious/moral IDIOMS (like Ram Rajya, ahimsa, satya) that ordinary Indians could readily UNDERSTAND and relate to. By living simply, identifying with the poor, and speaking in terms rooted in common life and morality, Gandhi bridged the gap between the elite leadership and the masses. So his simplicity and use of relatable symbols/language helped him mobilise the masses. So option 1 is correct.

stem: How did many ordinary people/peasants often PERCEIVE Gandhi, according to the chapter?
options: As a kind of saintly, almost divine figure with miraculous powers (a 'Mahatma'), around whom many rumours and stories grew
As an ordinary lawyer with no special status
solution: The chapter highlights that many ordinary people, especially PEASANTS, often perceived Gandhi in an exalted, almost RELIGIOUS way — as a saintly, semi-divine figure, a 'MAHATMA' ('great soul') endowed with extraordinary or even miraculous powers. Numerous RUMOURS and STORIES grew around him (e.g., that he could perform miracles, or that those who defied or opposed him would suffer). People interpreted him through their own cultural and religious frameworks, investing him with a charismatic, saviour-like aura. This popular perception (partly independent of Gandhi's own self-image) was an important source of his mass appeal. So peasants often saw him as a saintly, miraculous Mahatma. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India finally achieved independence on __________, though it was accompanied by the Partition and communal violence.
solution: India achieved independence on 15 August 1947, ending nearly two centuries of British rule. However, freedom came ALONGSIDE the PARTITION of the subcontinent into India and Pakistan, which was accompanied by horrific COMMUNAL VIOLENCE and one of the largest mass migrations in history. Gandhi, distressed by the communal carnage, was not celebrating in Delhi but working to restore peace (e.g., in Bengal). (He was assassinated on 30 January 1948.) So India became independent on 15 August 1947. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: Assertion (A): Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922. Reason (R): The movement had turned violent at Chauri Chaura, and Gandhi was committed to the principle of non-violence. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that Gandhi called off (suspended) the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922. And the reason is (R) that the movement had turned VIOLENT at Chauri Chaura (where a mob killed policemen by burning a police station), and Gandhi was deeply committed to the principle of NON-VIOLENCE (ahimsa) — he believed a struggle that had become violent was going wrong and must be halted. So his commitment to non-violence, in the face of the Chauri Chaura violence, directly explains why he called off the movement (A). So R correctly explains A. This is a prelims-relevant cause-and-effect.

stem: Assertion (A): Gandhi emphasised khadi and the charkha (spinning wheel). Reason (R): He saw hand-spinning and khadi as symbols of self-reliance, the dignity of labour, and national unity, and as a means to boycott British cloth. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that Gandhi strongly emphasised khadi (hand-spun, hand-woven cloth) and the charkha (spinning wheel). And the reason is (R) that he saw hand-spinning and khadi as powerful SYMBOLS of SELF-RELIANCE (economic independence from British textiles), the DIGNITY of manual LABOUR, and NATIONAL UNITY, and as a practical MEANS of BOYCOTTING British/machine-made cloth (thereby striking at the economic basis of colonial rule while building indigenous self-sufficiency). These meanings and purposes directly explain WHY he emphasised khadi and the charkha (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The chapter, in discussing how historians study Gandhi and the movement, stresses the importance of reading sources critically because __________.
options: Every source (official records, newspapers, letters, autobiographies) reflects a particular perspective and purpose, and a full, balanced picture emerges only by weighing and cross-checking many kinds of evidence
There is only one perfectly reliable source
Sources should be accepted without question
History can be written without any sources
solution: In discussing how we come to KNOW about Gandhi and the national movement, the chapter stresses reading sources CRITICALLY, because EVERY kind of source reflects a particular PERSPECTIVE and PURPOSE: official/government records give the colonial administration's view (often hostile or surveillance-oriented); newspapers vary by their political stance; private letters and autobiographies reveal personal views but are shaped by self-presentation; and popular perceptions carry their own interpretations. Since no single source is complete or perfectly objective, a FULL and BALANCED picture emerges only by WEIGHING and CROSS-CHECKING many kinds of evidence against one another. So sources must be read critically because each is partial and perspectival. So option 1 is correct. This is the chapter's key methodological theme.

stem: Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 at __________ in Gujarat.
solution: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 at Porbandar, a coastal town in Gujarat (his father was a diwan/minister there). His birthday, 2 October, is commemorated as Gandhi Jayanti in India and as the International Day of Non-Violence. So Gandhi was born at Porbandar. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The ashram Gandhi established near Ahmedabad, from which the Dandi/Salt March began in 1930, was the __________.
solution: The Sabarmati Ashram (on the banks of the Sabarmati river near Ahmedabad, Gujarat) was the ashram Gandhi established and lived in for many years, and from which he began the historic Salt/Dandi March in 1930. (Earlier, in South Africa, he had founded the Phoenix Settlement and Tolstoy Farm; later in life he set up the Sevagram Ashram near Wardha.) So the ashram from which the Salt March began was the Sabarmati Ashram. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The Non-Cooperation Movement was combined with the Khilafat movement. The Khilafat issue concerned __________.
options: The demand to protect the position of the Ottoman Sultan/Caliph (Khalifa) of Turkey after the First World War, a cause important to Indian Muslims
solution: The Khilafat movement concerned the demand to PROTECT the position and authority of the Ottoman Sultan of Turkey, who was the Caliph (Khalifa) — the spiritual head of the Muslim world — after the Ottoman Empire's defeat in the First World War (Indian Muslims feared the harsh peace terms would dismember the Ottoman empire and undermine the Caliphate). Gandhi and the Congress joined hands with the Khilafat leaders (like the Ali brothers), combining the Khilafat cause with Non-Cooperation to forge HINDU–MUSLIM UNITY in a joint struggle against the British. So the Khilafat issue concerned the Ottoman Caliph. This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: The demand for 'Purna Swaraj' (complete independence) was adopted by the Congress at its __________ session in 1929, and 26 January 1930 was observed as Independence Day.
solution: At the Lahore session of the Indian National Congress in December 1929 (presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru), the Congress adopted the demand for 'PURNA SWARAJ' — complete/full independence — as its goal. It was decided that 26 January 1930 would be observed as 'Independence Day' (Purna Swaraj Day) across the country. (This is why 26 January was later chosen as the date to inaugurate the Republic in 1950.) So the Purna Swaraj resolution was at the Lahore session (1929). This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The pact signed in 1931 between Gandhi and the Viceroy, under which the Civil Disobedience Movement was suspended and Gandhi agreed to attend the Round Table Conference, was the __________.
solution: The Gandhi–Irwin Pact was signed in March 1931 between Mahatma Gandhi and the Viceroy Lord Irwin. Under it, Gandhi agreed to SUSPEND the Civil Disobedience Movement and to attend the (Second) Round Table Conference in London, while the government agreed to release political prisoners and make certain concessions (such as allowing the making of salt for personal use in coastal areas). So the 1931 pact was the Gandhi–Irwin Pact. (The Poona Pact of 1932, by contrast, was between Gandhi and Ambedkar on the question of separate electorates/reserved seats for the depressed classes.) This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The series of conferences held in London (1930–32) to discuss constitutional reforms for India, which Gandhi attended (the second one) representing the Congress, were the __________.
solution: The Round Table Conferences were a series of three conferences held in London (1930–1932) by the British government to discuss constitutional reforms for India. Gandhi attended the SECOND Round Table Conference (1931) as the sole representative of the Congress (following the Gandhi–Irwin Pact), but it ended without agreement (partly over the question of communal/minority representation). So the London conferences were the Round Table Conferences. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The 1932 agreement between Gandhi and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar concerning the political representation of the depressed classes (reserving seats for them within the general electorate instead of separate electorates) was the __________.
solution: The Poona Pact (September 1932) was the agreement between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar (representing the depressed classes). The British had proposed SEPARATE ELECTORATES for the depressed classes (in the Communal Award); Gandhi opposed this (fearing it would divide Hindu society) and undertook a fast unto death. The Poona Pact resolved the impasse: separate electorates were given up in favour of RESERVED SEATS for the depressed classes within the general (joint) electorate, with an increased number of reserved seats. So the 1932 Gandhi–Ambedkar agreement was the Poona Pact. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, a leader of the depressed classes, differed with Gandhi mainly over __________.
options: The method of ending untouchability and securing rights for the depressed classes — Ambedkar demanded separate political safeguards/electorates and structural change, distrusting reliance on the goodwill of caste Hindus
solution: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, himself from a community treated as 'untouchable' and a champion of the depressed classes, differed with Gandhi mainly over the METHOD of ending untouchability and securing the rights and dignity of the depressed classes. Ambedkar demanded firm POLITICAL SAFEGUARDS (such as separate electorates and, later, reserved seats) and structural/social change, and he was sceptical of relying on the goodwill and reform of caste Hindus (as Gandhi's 'Harijan' approach seemed to). Gandhi, while opposing untouchability, opposed separate electorates for the depressed classes (fearing division of Hindu society), leading to their clash (resolved by the Poona Pact). So they differed over the method of securing depressed-class rights. So option 1 is correct. This is an important point.

stem: Gandhi was assassinated on 30 January 1948 in New Delhi by __________.
solution: Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated on 30 January 1948 at Birla House in New Delhi (during his evening prayer meeting) by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu extremist who was opposed to Gandhi's stance on communal harmony and his perceived favouring of Muslims/Pakistan (especially amid the Partition violence). Gandhi's death shocked the nation and the world. So he was assassinated by Nathuram Godse. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: In the last phase of his life, during the Partition riots (1946–48), Gandhi was engaged in __________.
options: Touring riot-affected areas (like Noakhali in Bengal, and Delhi) to restore communal peace and stop Hindu–Muslim violence, often fasting for peace
solution: In the last, tragic phase of his life, as India moved toward independence amid the horrific communal violence of Partition (1946–48), Gandhi was engaged in TOURING the riot-affected areas — such as Noakhali (in Bengal), Bihar, Calcutta, and later Delhi — walking from village to village to RESTORE COMMUNAL PEACE, comfort victims of both communities, and STOP the Hindu–Muslim VIOLENCE. He undertook FASTS for peace (e.g., in Calcutta and Delhi). He did not join the independence celebrations of 15 August 1947, instead working to quell the carnage. So in his last phase he worked to restore communal peace. So option 1 is correct.

stem: One important source for reconstructing Gandhi's role is the private correspondence and papers of the nationalist leaders. Historians must remember that letters were __________.
options: Sometimes meant to be private and sometimes written for eventual publication, so the writer's awareness of the audience shapes what is said — requiring careful, critical reading
Always completely spontaneous and unedited truth
solution: The private correspondence and papers of Gandhi and other nationalist leaders are important sources for reconstructing the movement. But historians must remember that LETTERS vary in nature: some were meant to be strictly PRIVATE (revealing candid thoughts), while others were written with an eye to EVENTUAL PUBLICATION or a wider audience (and so were more guarded, self-conscious, or crafted). The writer's AWARENESS of the (present or future) audience shapes what is said and how. Therefore letters must be read CAREFULLY and CRITICALLY, taking account of who they were written to and for, rather than being treated as unmediated truth. So option 1 is correct. This is a key methodological point about using letters as sources.

stem: The 'Salt March' (Dandi March) was a masterstroke of political mobilisation partly because it __________.
options: Was covered widely (including by the international press), dramatised the moral challenge to British rule, and drew people into the movement through a simple, symbolic act of defiance
Involved only Gandhi and no one else
Had nothing to do with British law
solution: The Salt March of 1930 was a masterstroke of political mobilisation and communication. By marching openly and slowly (over 240 miles, drawing crowds and attention at every stop) to Dandi to break the salt law, Gandhi staged a highly VISIBLE, dramatic act that was widely COVERED by the Indian and INTERNATIONAL PRESS — putting the moral case against British rule before the whole world. The march DRAMATISED the injustice of colonial rule through a simple, universally understood SYMBOL (salt), and it DREW ordinary people into the movement by inviting them to participate in an easy, symbolic act of defiance (making/selling salt). This combination of moral force, symbolism, and publicity made it enormously effective. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Women participated in large numbers in the movements led by Gandhi, especially during Civil Disobedience. This was significant because it __________.
options: Brought women out of the domestic sphere into public political life on an unprecedented scale, marking an important step for women's participation in the national movement
Had no effect on women's status
solution: Women participated in LARGE NUMBERS in the movements led by Gandhi — especially during the Civil Disobedience Movement (picketing liquor and foreign-cloth shops, making and selling salt, courting arrest, joining marches and protests). This was highly SIGNIFICANT because it brought women OUT of the domestic/private sphere into PUBLIC political life on an unprecedented scale, giving them an active role in the freedom struggle and marking an important step in women's political awakening and participation. Gandhi actively ENCOURAGED women's involvement (seeing qualities like courage and self-sacrifice in them). So women's mass participation was a significant step. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly lists the three major Gandhian mass movements in chronological order?
solution: The three major Gandhian mass movements, in chronological order, are: the NON-COOPERATION Movement (1920–22), the CIVIL DISOBEDIENCE Movement (launched 1930 with the Salt March; with a second phase 1932–34), and the QUIT INDIA Movement (1942). Knowing this sequence (and the key features of each) is prelims-critical. So option 1 gives the correct order.

stem: Gandhi's concept of 'Swaraj' meant more than just political independence; it also included __________.
options: Self-rule in a deeper sense — self-reliance, moral and social regeneration, the upliftment of the poor and oppressed, and rule that was just and rooted in Indian values (self-governance of both the nation and the self)
The rule of the British with Indian advisers
Only the transfer of power to elite Indians
solution: For Gandhi, 'SWARAJ' (self-rule) meant much MORE than merely the transfer of political power from British to Indian hands. It carried a DEEPER meaning: SELF-RELIANCE (economic and social self-sufficiency, symbolised by khadi and village industry); MORAL and SOCIAL regeneration (including the removal of untouchability, communal harmony, and ethical living); the UPLIFTMENT of the poor, peasants, and oppressed; and rule that was JUST and rooted in Indian values (his ideal of 'Ram Rajya'). It also implied self-governance of the SELF — self-discipline and self-mastery — not just of the nation. So Gandhi's swaraj included self-reliance and moral/social regeneration, not just political independence. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The chapter notes that Gandhi's message and image were spread not only by his own words but also by __________.
options: The way ordinary people, local leaders, newspapers, and rumour interpreted and popularised him (sometimes in ways he did not intend or control)
The British government's official propaganda alone
Radio broadcasts by the British only
solution: The chapter notes that Gandhi's MESSAGE and IMAGE were spread not only by his OWN words and actions but also — importantly — by the way OTHERS interpreted and popularised him: ORDINARY people (especially peasants) who invested him with saintly/miraculous qualities and spread STORIES and RUMOURS about him; LOCAL LEADERS and activists who carried his message (sometimes reshaping it to local contexts and grievances); and NEWSPAPERS and word of mouth. As a result, the 'Mahatma' that reached the masses was partly a POPULAR CONSTRUCTION — and people sometimes acted in his name in ways he did NOT intend or approve of. So his image was shaped by how others interpreted and spread it. So option 1 is correct. This is an important point about how the Mahatma's charisma worked.

stem: The First World War (1914–18) formed an important backdrop to the rise of the national movement because it __________.
options: Caused economic hardship (higher taxes, price rises, forced recruitment) and raised expectations of political reform, generating discontent that Gandhi's movements could tap
solution: The First World War (1914–18) formed an important backdrop to the rise of Gandhi's mass movements. The war caused considerable ECONOMIC HARDSHIP in India — higher taxes, rising PRICES (inflation) and shortages, and forced/aggressive RECRUITMENT of soldiers — which generated widespread DISCONTENT among peasants, workers, and others. At the same time, Indians' contributions to the war effort RAISED EXPECTATIONS of political REFORM and greater self-government, which were then disappointed (e.g., by the repressive Rowlatt Act instead). This accumulated discontent and disappointment created fertile conditions that Gandhi's movements (from 1919–20 onward) could TAP and mobilise. So the war generated hardship and discontent that fed the movement. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'constructive programme' that Gandhi promoted alongside political agitation included __________.
options: Promotion of khadi/village industries, removal of untouchability, Hindu–Muslim unity, basic education, sanitation, and the upliftment of villages
Building factories and railways for the British
solution: Alongside political AGITATION (the mass movements), Gandhi laid great stress on a 'CONSTRUCTIVE PROGRAMME' — positive, everyday social and economic work to build the nation from below and reform society. This included: the promotion of KHADI and VILLAGE INDUSTRIES (self-reliance); the REMOVAL of UNTOUCHABILITY; the fostering of HINDU–MUSLIM UNITY (communal harmony); BASIC (nai talim) EDUCATION; SANITATION and hygiene; the upliftment of VILLAGES, women, and the poor; and prohibition. Gandhi saw such constructive work as essential to genuine swaraj (moral and social regeneration), not merely a supplement to political struggle. So the constructive programme included khadi, anti-untouchability, communal unity, education, and village upliftment. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): Gandhi undertook fasts as a political and moral weapon. Reason (R): Fasting (self-suffering) was a means, consistent with non-violence, to appeal to the conscience of opponents and followers, to protest injustice, and to restore discipline or peace. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that Gandhi repeatedly undertook FASTS (including 'fasts unto death') as a political and moral weapon (e.g., against untouchability/separate electorates leading to the Poona Pact, to stop communal violence, and to restore discipline during agitations). And the reason is (R) that FASTING — voluntary SELF-SUFFERING — was, in Gandhi's philosophy, a means fully consistent with NON-VIOLENCE: by taking suffering upon HIMSELF (rather than inflicting it on others), he sought to APPEAL to the CONSCIENCE of his opponents and followers, to PROTEST injustice, and to RESTORE discipline or peace through moral pressure. So the nature and purpose of fasting as a non-violent, conscience-appealing tool directly explains why Gandhi used it (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): The national movement under Gandhi drew in peasants and workers on a large scale. Reason (R): Gandhi's simple lifestyle, use of familiar symbols and idioms, and identification with the poor made the movement accessible and appealing to the masses. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that under Gandhi the national movement drew in PEASANTS and WORKERS (and other ordinary people) on a large, unprecedented scale. And the reason is (R) that Gandhi's SIMPLE lifestyle and dress, his use of FAMILIAR SYMBOLS (khadi, charkha, salt) and religious/moral IDIOMS, and his IDENTIFICATION with the POOR made the movement ACCESSIBLE, relatable, and appealing to the masses (who could understand its message and participate in its methods). So Gandhi's simplicity and mass-oriented style directly explain the large-scale participation of peasants and workers (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The government/official records (like police reports and intelligence files) on Gandhi and the movement are useful to historians but biased because they __________.
options: Were produced by the colonial state to monitor, control, and suppress the movement, so they view Gandhi and the nationalists with suspicion/hostility and from the standpoint of surveillance
solution: The colonial GOVERNMENT/official records — police reports, intelligence and surveillance files, fortnightly reports, and correspondence — are useful sources (rich in detail about the movement's activities and the authorities' responses), but they are BIASED. They were produced by the COLONIAL STATE for the purposes of MONITORING, CONTROLLING, and SUPPRESSING the movement, so they view Gandhi and the nationalists with SUSPICION and HOSTILITY, from the standpoint of SURVEILLANCE and law-and-order. They tend to portray the movement as a threat and may downplay its popular support or moral appeal. Historians therefore read them critically, aware of this official, adversarial perspective. So official records are useful but biased by their surveillance/suppression purpose. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following best describes the RELATIONSHIP between Gandhi and the Indian National Congress?
options: Gandhi transformed the Congress into a mass organisation and became its guiding spirit, reshaping its methods, structure, and goals — though he was not always in formal office and did not always have his way
Gandhi had no connection with the Congress
The Congress was a British body Gandhi never joined
solution: Gandhi's relationship with the Indian National Congress was central and transformative. From around 1920, he TRANSFORMED the Congress from a body of the educated elite into a MASS ORGANISATION with a broad membership, a reorganised structure (down to the village level), and new methods (satyagraha, non-cooperation, the constructive programme) and goals (swaraj, later purna swaraj). He became its GUIDING SPIRIT and greatest leader — though he did not always hold formal OFFICE (he was Congress president only once, in 1924), and he did NOT always get his way (there were differences with other leaders and factions). So Gandhi transformed and guided the Congress as its central figure, without always being in office or unopposed. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The chapter's exploration of how we KNOW about Gandhi (through diverse and often conflicting sources) teaches the broader lesson that __________.
options: Writing history involves interpreting and weighing varied sources critically, being aware of each source's perspective, silences, and biases — history is a reasoned reconstruction, not a simple copying of any single account
History is just memorising one textbook
All sources agree, so interpretation is unnecessary
solution: By exploring HOW we come to know about Gandhi — through DIVERSE and sometimes CONFLICTING sources (newspapers of different leanings, hostile official records, personal letters and autobiographies, popular perceptions and rumours) — the chapter teaches a broader lesson about the DISCIPLINE of history: writing history involves INTERPRETING and WEIGHING varied sources CRITICALLY, being alert to each source's PERSPECTIVE, SILENCES, and BIASES, and reconstructing the past through reasoned judgement. History is thus a careful, critical RECONSTRUCTION built by evaluating evidence — NOT a simple copying or acceptance of any single account. So option 1 is correct. This meta-lesson (about the nature of historical knowledge) is a key aim of the chapter and of the whole book.

stem: The term 'Mahatma' applied to Gandhi means __________.
solution: The title 'MAHATMA' (Sanskrit: maha = great, atma = soul) means 'GREAT SOUL'. It was applied to Gandhi as a mark of the deep reverence in which he was held for his spiritual and moral greatness, his self-sacrifice, and his championing of truth and the poor. (The title is popularly associated with Rabindranath Tagore having used it for Gandhi.) So 'Mahatma' means 'great soul'. This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: Gandhi's insistence that the MEANS must be as pure as the ENDS (i.e., a just goal cannot be achieved through unjust/violent means) was a core principle underlying his politics. This reflects his belief in __________.
options: The inseparability of means and ends — that truth (satya) and non-violence (ahimsa) must govern the methods of struggle, not just its aims
The idea that any means are justified by the end
The irrelevance of morality to politics
solution: A core principle of Gandhi's politics was the INSEPARABILITY of MEANS and ENDS — his firm belief that the means employed must be as PURE and just as the ends sought, and that a good/just goal (like freedom) CANNOT legitimately be achieved through unjust, immoral, or VIOLENT means. For Gandhi, TRUTH (satya) and NON-VIOLENCE (ahimsa) had to govern the METHODS of struggle, not merely its aims — indeed, the means were seen as the 'seed' and the end the 'tree'. This is why he insisted on non-violent satyagraha and called off movements (like Non-Cooperation) that turned violent. So this reflects his belief in the inseparability of means and ends (rejecting 'the end justifies the means'). So option 1 is correct.

stem: Overall, why is Gandhi regarded as such a pivotal figure in modern Indian history?
options: He merely gave speeches with no lasting effect

He gave the freedom struggle a mass base, a distinctive moral method (non-violent satyagraha), and a broad vision (swaraj, social reform, communal unity), inspiring not only India's independence but movements for justice and non-violence worldwide
He was important only in South Africa
solution: Gandhi is regarded as a pivotal figure in modern Indian history because he fundamentally shaped the freedom struggle and left a lasting legacy: he gave the movement a genuine MASS BASE (mobilising peasants, workers, women, and ordinary people); he pioneered a distinctive, MORAL METHOD of struggle — NON-VIOLENT SATYAGRAHA (truth-force) — that offered a powerful alternative to both submission and armed revolt; and he articulated a broad VISION of swaraj that fused political freedom with SOCIAL REFORM (against untouchability), economic self-reliance, and COMMUNAL UNITY. His leadership was central to India's attainment of INDEPENDENCE (1947), and his philosophy of non-violence went on to INSPIRE movements for civil rights, justice, and peace around the WORLD (e.g., Martin Luther King Jr., Nelson Mandela). So Gandhi was pivotal for his mass method, moral vision, and global influence. So option 2 is correct.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement' is that:
options: Gandhi had little impact on India's freedom struggle

Mahatma Gandhi (after returning from South Africa in 1915) became the towering leader of the Indian national movement, transforming it into a mass struggle through his method of non-violent satyagraha — from early campaigns (Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad) through the great movements of Non-Cooperation (1920–22), Civil Disobedience (the Salt/Dandi March, 1930), and Quit India (1942) — mobilising peasants, workers, women, and ordinary people with simple symbols (khadi, charkha, salt) and moral ideals (truth, non-violence, Hindu-Muslim unity, and the removal of untouchability), and being revered by the masses as a saintly 'Mahatma'; and the chapter also teaches how historians reconstruct his life and the movement from varied sources (newspapers, official records, letters, autobiographies), which must be read critically
The movement was led entirely by the British
solution: The chapter's overall message is that Mahatma Gandhi was the TOWERING and transformative leader of the Indian national movement in the decades before independence. After returning from South Africa in 1915 (where he had forged the method of SATYAGRAHA — non-violent resistance based on truth), he rose to lead the freedom struggle and TRANSFORMED it into a genuine MASS MOVEMENT. Beginning with early, localised satyagrahas (Champaran 1917 for indigo peasants, Kheda 1918 for revenue relief, and the Ahmedabad mill-workers' dispute), he went on to lead the great all-India movements: NON-COOPERATION (1920–22, combined with the Khilafat cause, called off after the Chauri Chaura violence), CIVIL DISOBEDIENCE (launched with the Salt/Dandi March of 1930 against the salt law), and finally QUIT INDIA (1942, with the call 'Do or Die'). He drew PEASANTS, WORKERS, WOMEN, and ordinary people of all classes and regions into the struggle, using SIMPLE, powerful SYMBOLS (khadi and the charkha, salt) and MORAL/religious IDEALS (truth, ahimsa/non-violence, Hindu–Muslim unity, and the campaign against untouchability, calling the 'untouchables' Harijans) — living simply, identifying with the poor, and being revered by the masses as a saintly 'MAHATMA'. Independence finally came in 1947 (though tragically accompanied by Partition and communal violence). Crucially, the chapter also teaches HOW historians reconstruct Gandhi's life and the movement — from VARIED SOURCES such as newspapers, government/official records, private letters, and autobiographies — each of which reflects a particular perspective and must be read CRITICALLY and cross-checked. So the overall message is option 2.
